findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph (desktop and phone), and the 'Graded for the site' image in the Texture section
findings.fault: The direction asks for a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking, graded into the house blue-grey. Instead, the photo's backdrop has been cut away and Mark sits as a cutout on flat slate. His skin, suit and red tie keep their full colour, so he is not graded into the ground. The cut shows: there is a light fringe around his hair on desktop, and a jagged diagonal edge where the lectern meets the backdrop in the Texture image. The result reads as a head pasted onto a colour field. It does not read as Mark at work in real light. (This is about the cutout treatment, not the stand-in photo's crop or quality.)
findings.who_objects: The founder. The research behind v7 calls for real people in real light, with imagery graded into the house colours, and it names 'slick' as a failure. A pasted-in cutout looks like the corporate headshot any consultancy could run, and it takes away the 'at work' context that is this direction's whole lever.

findings.where: Article specimen, the numbers of the ordered list (1, 2, 3)
findings.fault: The list numbers are set in the house blue, the link colour, but they are not links. The specimen's own note says 'blue only where something can be clicked', and the palette table also lists 'list numbers' under blue. So the page breaks its own rule.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned on this page that blue means clickable, and who taps the numbers and gets nothing. Angélique would also object: the article template is hers to keep, and it teaches her two meanings for one colour.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row with the PDF icon at the end of the post
findings.fault: A different piece ('Streamlining the PPP Process… Lecture · 23 April 2026') sits straight under the blog post's last line. Nothing labels it as related or further reading. Its download icon and 'PDF' label suggest it is this post's own download. Its title is also set about 4 px in from the column edge that the body text and rules share.
findings.who_objects: A bank staffer finishing the article would wonder whether this is the PDF of what they just read, and could download the wrong document. The download icon also promises a straight file, where the trust rules want a PDF behind an HTML page.

findings.where: First screen, the name and logo at top left (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: His name is set small, in regular-weight serif, beside a much larger bright-white aqueduct mark. When you squint, the firm's mark wins over his name. The name is also static (the parts map), while the mark beside it is the home link, which is the opposite of what visitors expect from the name at top left.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test says 'his name leads, with the logo beside it'. Here the name only leads in reading order, not in weight. A visitor who clicks the name to go home also gets nothing.

findings.where: First screen, the logo reversed to warm white on slate
findings.fault: The mark and wordmark have been recoloured to a white version on the slate ground. The client holds no such version and has not approved one, and the brand sheet gives the wordmark as the house blue.
findings.who_objects: Mark, the client, whose logo is shown in colours he never approved. The house rule says a white version is made only with the client's yes, and the founder has to answer for that.

findings.where: First screen nav: Profile, Articles and talks, Blog
findings.fault: All three nav links go to the same place, the article specimen (#article). 'Profile' lands the visitor on a blog post. The nav also has no 'Contact' item.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor from a development bank who clicks Profile to check Mark's record and gets an essay instead. The trust rules also expect a 'Contact' label in the navigation, alongside the address in the footer.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Placeholder: Mark's photo…' caption (desktop bottom left, phone under the action)
findings.fault: The photo's caption sits at the far left under the text column, away from the photo it describes on the right. On phone it sits under the email box, well below the photo. By proximity it reads as a note about the text or the action, not the picture.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first: the caption doesn't clearly attach to the photograph it is meant to flag.

findings.where: Article specimen heading 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', and the word spacing after full stops in Newsreader text ('being written.The PPP', 'long reading.Weight 330')
findings.fault: The display heading uses a straight apostrophe, while the body uses curly quotes (‘chapter topics’). Also, the space after some full stops nearly disappears, so those sentences look as if the space is missing.
findings.who_objects: Readers of a legal-journal-quality page, and Mark himself, a lawyer by background: both would read these as typos in a page meant to look refined.

findings.where: Texture section (desktop): the two comparison images
findings.fault: The two images and their note fill only the left two thirds of the column, and the right third is empty. Other sections (Type pair, Motion sketch) use both columns.
findings.who_objects: A designer reviewing the tile: this one section looks unfinished next to its neighbours, which hurts the 'alive, not boring' ask.
